props.title: Don't Bother to Knock

sections.content: **Don't Bother to Knock** (1952) marks Marilyn Monroe's first dramatic leading role, delivering a haunting performance as Nell Forbes, a mentally unstable babysitter. The film's claustrophobic setting - almost entirely within a single hotel - creates a pressure cooker atmosphere reminiscent of **The Night of the Hunter** (1955) and early Hitchcock works like **Shadow of a Doubt** (1943). Director Roy Ward Baker transforms the Waldorf Hotel into a noir playground of shadows and paranoia, while Richard Widmark brings his trademark intensity as the cynical pilot Jed Towers.

sections.content: The film represents a crucial turning point in Monroe's career, proving she could handle complex dramatic roles beyond the "dumb blonde" typecasting. Her portrayal of mental illness is remarkably nuanced for 1952, predating other groundbreaking performances like Anthony Perkins in **Psycho** (1960) and Gene Tierney in **Leave Her to Heaven** (1945). The confined hotel setting became a noir staple, later influencing films like **The Lodger** (1944) and **Elevator to the Gallows** (1958).

Baker's direction employs innovative techniques for the era, using tight close-ups and Dutch angles to heighten psychological tension. The film's exploration of post-war trauma and mental health issues was ahead of its time, connecting thematically to later works like **Shock Corridor** (1963) and **The Snake Pit** (1948). Anne Bancroft makes her film debut here, adding another layer of exceptional performance to this overlooked noir gem. SUBHEAD: Film Noir's Psychological Turn

sections.content: **Don't Bother to Knock** represents film noir's shift toward psychological thriller territory, moving away from straightforward crime stories. This evolution influenced later masterpieces like **Repulsion** (1965) and **Images** (1972). The film's treatment of mental illness, while dated by modern standards, was revolutionary for showing sympathy toward its troubled protagonist rather than depicting them as simply villainous.
